props.title: Heading South
props.initialSlug: Sex tourism and power games in 1970s Haiti

sections.content: Heading South marks a pivotal exploration of female sexual tourism and post-colonial power dynamics in Haiti. Director Laurent Cantet crafts a provocative drama that shares thematic DNA with Paradise: Love (2012) and How Stella Got Her Groove Back (1998), but takes a darker, more critical stance. Charlotte Rampling delivers a masterful performance as Ellen, capturing the complex intersection of privilege, desire, and willful ignorance against the backdrop of Papa Doc Duvalier's oppressive regime. The film's unflinching examination of exploitation parallels later works like White Material (2009) in its critique of lingering colonial attitudes.

sections.content: Cantet's approach builds on the tradition of European filmmakers examining Caribbean colonial aftermath, reminiscent of I Am Cuba (1964) and The Last Supper (1976). But where those films focused on revolutionary politics, Heading South zeroes in on intimate power dynamics. The film's 1970s setting allows it to examine both personal and political exploitation through the lens of wealthy Western women seeking sexual relationships with young Haitian men, while the country crumbles under dictatorship.

The film's visual language deserves special attention, with cinematographer Pierre Milon creating a stark contrast between sun-drenched tourist spaces and the shadowy reality of Haitian life under Duvalier. This technique would later influence films like Sugar (2008) and Our Day Will Come (2010) in their examination of Caribbean-Western relations. The resort setting becomes a metaphorical borderland where privilege and poverty collide. SUBHEAD: Sexual Politics and Power

sections.content: Rampling's Ellen represents a complex evolution in cinema's portrayal of female sexual desire, particularly in later life. The film's treatment of this theme creates interesting dialogue with works like The Swimming Pool (2003) and 45 Years (2015), both also starring Rampling. But where those films explore desire within European contexts, Heading South adds layers of economic and racial power dynamics that complicate every interaction.
